subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has exempted lumber, unprocessed fish, and beer from the trade deal with the United States, but not water. Despite claims to the contrary by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), it is obvious that the trade deal does not explicitly prohibit the sale of water to the United States. Therefore, we do not know what the future might hold with respect to water diversions and export.
By not exempting water from the trade deal, the Government has left the door open for the United States to seek Canadian water in decades to come. If the Government will not amend the proposed legislation so as to exclude water from the trade deal, the consequences could be enormous.
The Government should include water in the proposed trade legislation so that Canadian water stays in Canada for present and future generations of Canadians

speechtext:

subtopic: "THEY HAVE REACHED THE SUMMIT" COMPETITION-SCARCITY OF FEMALE WINNERS DEPLORED
"THEY HAVE REACHED THE SUMMIT" COMPETITION-SCARCITY OF FEMALE WINNERS DEPLORED
speechtext:
Earlier this week, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Youth announced the winners of the "They have reached the Summit" competition. Fifteen out of 1,000 young Canadian men and women were chosen to attend the Economic Summit in Toronto this weekend.
This kind of competition seems to offer a unique opportunity to young Canadians. However the distressing fact is that only three of the fifteen winners are women. Whenever this Government has an opportunity to offer young people a challenging experience it continues to perpetuate a sexist system which invariably bars women from institutions where political and economic decisions are made. It is very discouraging to find out that even today young Canadian women have no guarantee they will have equal representation and participation in our country's major events.
I want to extend my congratulations to the competition winners, particularly to the three young women. The name of the competition-"They have reached the Summit"-was quite appropriate, even though so few women did reach the top.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION BELL CANADA EXTENDED AREA SERVICE-DELAY IN ANNOUNCING DECISION
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION BELL CANADA EXTENDED AREA SERVICE-DELAY IN ANNOUNCING DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed to learn that the CRTC has once again delayed the announcement of its decision concerning extended area service of Bell Canada.
The residents of the northern part of the new riding of Markham with telephone exchanges 727 and 841 are only able to make local calls to Oak Ridges, Aurora, and Newmarket, whereas many calls must be made regularly to the greater Metro area. Residents such as Roy Graham have been fighting to get this changed.
I now live in the Gormley area. We have an 841 exchange. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is inconvenient and costly for residents to make calls to the greater Metro area. Almost all the calls are to the south, not to the west and north. This patchwork quilt of rates is particularly costly to small businesses with clients across the York region.
I would urge the CRTC to examine its criteria in order to apply the extended area service to our community and to many others across the province.

subtopic: LEVEL OF LEAD IN GASOLINE-QUICKER REDUCTION SOUGHT
LEVEL OF LEAD IN GASOLINE-QUICKER REDUCTION SOUGHT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday a group called the Canadian Coalition for Lead-Free Gasoline presented a brief to the federal Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan).
In the brief the Coalition outlined the dangers, especially to young children, of lead poisoning. The Coalition presented evidence that even very small levels of lead in the bloodstream can hurt children, and have terrible effects such as low birth weight and hearing loss. Fifty-two per cent of children aged six and under have an unacceptably high level of lead in their blood. That is half a million Canadian children.
To combat this problem, the Coalition has asked the Government to reduce the level of lead in gasoline sooner than the Government's plan to reduce levels in 1992. Why should the Conservative Government drag its feet when the health of Canadian children is at stake?
The Minister of the Environment expressed a concern for the industries, saying that the Government would have to ask the industries if they could meet this target for reducing lead at an earlier date.
It is time this Conservative Government got the lead out, and told the industries to do the same.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM SIZED BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as of June 3, the Western Diversification Office had provided funds for 382 projects across western Canada. These announcements have amounted to $305 million being injected into western Canada. It is important to realize that the vast majority of the projects funded are for small and medium-sized companies. These are the companies which create most of the jobs and are the driving force in diversifying the prairie economy. These companies have the entrepreneurs who bring new ideas and skills to both rural and urban areas.
An example of the impact that ingenuity and government support is having can be found in Saskatoon East. A Saskatoon engineer's unique mining conveyor system will become a reality with the help of western diversification funds. As a result of this co-operation up to 1,000 new jobs could be created in businesses over the next three to four years. This is an example of how individuals can build innovative and highly competitive industries while providing growth and development in Saskatchewan.
The western diversification initiative is beginning to enhance the development of a broadly based western economy. It is promising a brighter future for the west.

subsubtopic: VETERANS INDEPENDENCE PROGRAM-ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are indeed fortunate in this country in having an outstanding Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees). His understanding and compassion for this country's veterans, and his persuasive abilities with his cabinet colleagues, have resulted in unprecedented new initiatives to recognize and assist those men and women who have served Canada so well.
For example, at the Dominion Convention of the Royal Canadian Legion this week, the Minister announced that an additional $200 million has been approved by the Government in order that those veterans who served at least one year during wartime in Canada will be eligible for the Veterans Independence Program.
This will more than double the number of veterans who will be potentially eligible for the Veterans Independence Program which ensures that veterans receive assistance to help them remain independent in their own homes. He also announced that the Government has agreed to provide more chronic care facilities in order that, when needed by veterans, the beds will be available.

It is these efforts by this Government which are ensuring that our veterans face their future with dignity and security.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO MINISTER'S COMMENTS IN REPLYING TO QUESTION ON RAPE
speechtext:

It is reported that Liberal Members of the Legislature applauded.
The Minister's levity betrays a profound and distressing insensitivity to the issue of rape. Each year thousands of Canadian women are the victims of sexual assault, a violent crime that should not and must not be trivialized.
Mr. Sorbara, Minister responsible for women's issues in the Ontario Government, owes the women of Canada an apology, and I call on the Premier of Ontario and the Liberal Party of Canada publicly to disavow this Minister's comments and attitude.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ROLE OF CANADIAN TRADE COMMISSIONERS
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ROLE OF CANADIAN TRADE COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. I have a copy of a memo from the Department of External Affairs outlining the Government's massive propaganda sale of the Canada-U.S. trade deal.
The Prime Minister has stated, as has the Minister, that this trade deal will be part of the next election. We also know that


the legislation has not passed Parliament and that there is a very divisive debate across the country.
Yet the memo clearly outlines that not only will the Government be spending millions of dollars, it will now be requiring public servants, including all the trade commissioners presently in the United States, to be flown to Canada at taxpayers' expense to team up with Conservative Members of Parliament to attend meetings across the country to sell the trade deal as part of that election platform.
How can the Minister possibly justify not only the outrageous waste of taxpayers' money but an attempt to force public servants to appear for blatant election political purposes? Does he not clearly consider this to be a destruction of the independence of the Canadian Public Service?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ROLE OF CANADIAN TRADE COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apparently the Hon. Member has never heard of the fact that Canada has an export promotion program and we have been spending tens and tens and tens of millions of dollars in Canada for many years now to promote our exports. Since just about 80 per cent of our exports go to the United States of America, much of that money is spent on promoting exports to the United States of America, which is what we are doing in our campaign which will start next week With a series of 17 seminars across Canada. We will invite Canadian businessmen to them and the theme of these seminars is how they can increase their exports to take advantage of the opportunities of the free trade agreement.
Is there any point in negotiating a free trade agreement which starts next January 1 unless we encourage Canadian businesses, large and small, to take advantage of it, to see where the opportunities are and to follow up on them? We have had studies done now of 30 industrial sectors in which Canadians can increase exports to the United States, and we are spending the money on that purpose. It has nothing to do with the promotion of the free trade agreement, but it does show how valuable the free trade agreement is to Canada and Canadians.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-ROLE OF CANADIAN TRADE COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just remind the Minister that the trade deal is by no means a fait accompli. It has not been passed by Parliament yet, and he better not count his chickens until they hatch.

Three weeks ago, a public servant who works for Customs and Excise, Mr. Mike Clough, was give a written warning from the Government that he would face disciplinary action if he attended a meeting to debate the trade issue in opposition to the Canada-U.S. trade deal. How can the Government on the one hand justify gagging certain public servants who oppose this agreement while on the other hand it forces other public servants to go in attendance with Conservative Members of Parliament to sell the deal? Why the double standard? Why are public servants only given the right to speak on this crucial issue when they support the Government's message?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
speechtext: That's false.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is nothing in the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement that forces Canada to sell water to anyone or to sell anything to anyone.

Liberal Party Members seem to think that we ought to stop government assistance to the regions whenever there is an election. That argument does not hold, it does not make sense. I do not think they would have done that in the past and I fail to see why Lac-Saint-Jean residents should be penalized because of the by-election in their riding.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, you will notice that the Minister doesn't know under what program the job creation centre in Alma was announced. The Minister doesn't know either when work on the airport will be carried out. It is clear that all these announcements were made only to attract votes. I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister when he will finally have the decency to stop these million-dollar promises which are being made for only one purpose, and that is to buy votes. What do you think the people of Lac-Saint-Jean are?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party must be afraid of Lac-Saint-Jean. You must be afraid of what is going to happen there. During the last three years, 18,000 jobs were created in Lac-Saint-Jean. Did the Liberal Party ever rise during that time to congratulate the Government or to accuse us of wanting to buy votes? Economic prosperity is coming back to Quebec's resource regions, and the Liberal Party deplores that fact. For sixteen years, Mr. Speaker, when the Liberal Party was in power, Lac-Saint-Jean was left to its own devices. Our Government is taking care of all the regions of this country and of all Quebec's resource regions, including Lac-Saint-Jean, and not because we are having a by-election, because this has been our policy since 1984.

subsubtopic: AIR ALMA-FATE OF ENTREPRISE AND ITS SIXTY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for Regional Industrial Expansion.
While the Prime Minister and his candidate in the Lac-Saint-Jean by-election are announcing regional economic development programs worth $1 billion, and while the Minister of Transport is distributing goodies in this riding, Air Alma may well be obliged to close down tomorrow, as result of competition from Inter Canadien.
What is the Minister going to do to save this local business and its 60 jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: AIR ALMA-FATE OF ENTREPRISE AND ITS SIXTY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know there would have been no problem for a socialist government, because it would nationalize everything. There would be no competititon. It would be a government...
In this case, the programs are in place. If under the Job Development or Job Strategy Program we can help workers that might be affected ... This is hypothetical, since I don't have the details. But I am sure there are programs to deal with this.
The Hon. Member also referred to the Regional Development Program. One billion dollars has been announced for this program, with the co-operation of the Government of Quebec. This is an important measure for Quebec's resource regions. I am pleased that the New Democratic Party realizes the value of this program. In the weeks to come, programs will be developed in various areas, and perhaps one of these new programs can be used to provide assistance in this particular case, but so far I don't know.

subtopic: QUERY WHETHER SITUATION WILL OCCUR IN OTHER REGIONS
QUERY WHETHER SITUATION WILL OCCUR IN OTHER REGIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the same Minister, the mouth-piece of patronage.
In January 1988, when deregulation came into effect, the Conservatives promised us better service at lower cost.
What is going on with Air Alma reflects exactly what we have seen with the Conservatives, the rich are getting richer while the poor are getting poorer.
Can the Minister tell us if what we are seeing in Lac Saint-Jean will happen in other remote areas, like Sept-Iles, and Rouyn-Noranda?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER SITUATION WILL OCCUR IN OTHER REGIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I hear those people saying that the "rich are getting richer, while the poor..." One thing is sure, in this country, since 1984, far less people are living below the poverty level than before. A lot more people are working than in 1984, when we were elected. And that holds true for every region in this country.
The Government has embarked on a regional development program and has made some considerable changes which have resulted in a healthier economy.
Back home, that means more money to send the children to school, more money for other projects.
So, the rhetoric of the Socialist Party may look terrific in print, but we have seen the results of its application in Manitoba. I don't think Canadians want a piece of it, and that is fine with us. We will continue to implement programs in Quebec and in other regions, just as we have done since 1984, programs which benefit all Canadians.

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-CROSSCOUNTRY SEMINARS-GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister for International Trade. In order to sell his free trade salad, the Minister has hired no less than six public relations firms to do the cross-Canada trips. That is in addition to the seventh firm, of course, which just happens to be run by his former campaign manager. What selection process was utilized to hire these firms which, by happy coincidence, resulted in the fact that Prime Public Relations Inc. run by Mr. Garry Watton, a well-known Conservative, got the contract in Newfoundland; that Saga Communications Ltd., which contributed $3,000 to the Conservative Party, got the contract for the Maritimes; that Basin, Dumas, Dupre and Sormany, which contributed $3,000, got the contract for Quebec, and so on? What happy coincidence led to this? And can the Minister indicate to this House approximately how much it will cost to reward the few Tories left in this country who have not yet been rewarded?

speechtext: The devil made you do it.

contributed to. Even if they contributed to the New Democratic Party, we would still consider their services.
In the meantime, there is someone called Garry Watton who is supposed to be a great Progressive Conservative down in Newfoundland. If so, I am delighted to hear about the man. I am going to welcome him as a new member the next time I see him. I have never met him in my life.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. The Minister said earlier, in answer to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, that this promotion campaign had nothing to do with promoting the free trade agreement, per se. Given that the press release sent by FAX all over the country states:
The conferences are being arranged in an incredibly short time frame and
will call for a maximum of flexibility, goodwill and last minute preparation by
our posts in the U.S.A., the regional trade offices-
And so on. Can the Minister tell the House if it is not a fact that the Government wants this program to be done quickly so it can get it over with before the election, so it can use this as political party propaganda designed to promote the Conservative Party and nothing else?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have seen an outline there of the Liberal philosophy and Liberal actions. The hon. gentleman exemplifies them in every word of suspicion he tries to transfer to someone else.
The agreement is going to go into effect on January 1. This is June. There are six months for us to ensure that every Canadian businessman, large and small, is advised of what his opportunities are in the United States.
There are 90 studies being done by the firm of Peat Marwick Mitchell on different sectors and industries in the United States to show how we will have an advantage under this agreement as compared to other countries so that we can sell where we are more competitive, and that is what we are doing.
We have six months to prepare. We would have had longer except for the obstruction on the other side, and the denigration on the other side, and the destructive tactics on the other side. But we are going to have 17 conferences now, and then 17 more, and then 17 more.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. It has now been about two weeks since we had the emergency debate here on the British fur labelling proposal. A number of Members on the government side, as well as from the Opposition, spoke on this matter and expressed their concern.
Given the concerns, given the number of jobs at stake, could the Minister tell the House what specific steps his Government has taken to convey the results of that debate to British parliamentarians and, in general, our concern here?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I responded to that question yesterday. It was posed by the Hon. Member for Timiskaming. There have indeed been representations made to the Prime Minister of Great Britain by the Prime Minister, and also representations made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Definitely, this issue will be raised during the bilateral discussions that the Prime Minister will have with Prime Minister Thatcher.
I should also indicate that I think there are consultations going on among the House Leaders right at this very moment about the possibility of this House moving a unanimous resolution that would reflect the spirit of the debate that took place a week ago. I hope that the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party would see fit to agree with this resolution so that it can be endorsed unanimously by all Members of the House. I think that that would send a very strong signal.

Mr. Speaker, I think that while the strong words that we have heard will be of some comfort to trappers and to the 105,000 members of the fur industry, they will not really address the problem. Strong words without strong actions are meaningless.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister tell us, in addition to diplomatic expressions of concern, what specific options or retaliatory measures he is proposing to the British Government should it undertake this labelling?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here again we are hearing some implied suggestions that there should be other actions taken. Perhaps the Hon. Member, if she is serious, would outline what the position of her Party is. The other day we heard the Leader of the New Democratic Party say that rather than defending our oceans, in particular in the north, we should engage in diplomatic rhetoric. It is quite a different position from what the Hon. Member is implying today.


We are taking very strong and vigorous action with regard to the representations that are being made. I call again on the Hon. Member and members of her Party to support the resolution that is being proposed by the Government and, hopefully, supported by the Liberals. I think that the unanimous support of such a resolution by the House of Commons would be the very strong united signal that we need to help in the bargaining process.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SOWETO UPRISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Today is the twelfth anniversary of the Soweto uprising when police opened fire on students in South Africa's biggest ghetto.
Will the Minister recognize that there is absolutely no end to repression in South Africa and, in the words of many, it must now be treated as nothing less than a terrorist state? Will the Minister agree to act on South Africa, to match the Prime Minister's rhetoric with the sort of measures that have been proposed by the Leader of the Opposition? Will the Government finally agree to call back permanently Canada's Ambassador and impose full economic sanctions on this terrorist state?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-TWELFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SOWETO UPRISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the country knows-certainly the House knows-of the actions that have been taken in the last three or four years by the Government, the Prime Minister, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to put pressure upon and to try to exert influence upon South Africa with respect to its apartheid policy.
I might point out to the hon. gentleman that his Government was in power for eight years out of those twelve, this being the twelfth anniversary of that event. Yet I cannot think of one single action his Government took or anything that it said during that time about the situation in South Africa, certainly nothing comparable to the actions of the last two or three years.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS FOR ECONOMIC BOYCOTT
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS FOR ECONOMIC BOYCOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister cannot take refuge in the past. A succession of events took place, as well as an escalation of violence that has not been accepted anywhere in the world. The commitments that have been made by the Prime Minister are quite clear. He said that if there was no progress he would end diplomatic relations with South Africa. He has been paying only lip-service thus far.
Oral Questions
I want to know from the Minister if the Prime Minister is going to use the summit in Toronto to raise the matter, and to impress upon the Prime Minister of Britain and the President of the United States to act in concert and, indeed, to boycott South Africa effectively?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS FOR ECONOMIC BOYCOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the actions taken by Canada and the leadership that Canada has provided have been amply proved by the recognition accorded to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who was made the Chairman of the Commonwealth Group of Ministers acting in this matter. The Prime Minister's position has been recognized by the leaders of Zimbabwe and the front line States. The record is excellent.
We are now reviewing, and will continue to review, what is happening in South Africa and what our next steps should be, what can be most helpful, and what can be most useful to accomplish our objective which is to encourage South Africa to abolish the apartheid system and to treat its black citizens on an equal basis with all the rest of its citizens, of course the minority of whom are white citizens who have full privileges.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is addressed to the Deputy Prime Minister. As he knows, the Prime Minister as the host to the summit conference beginning Sunday has naturally expressed our pride in the Canadian traditions of democracy and free speech. Yet the Metro Toronto police have arrested a dozen students who were protesting peacefully at the University of Toronto overnight against the foreign and economic policies of the summit seven.
They have forbidden a peaceful protest march to use College Street, Yonge Street, King Street and University Street, all of which streets are outside the summit security area. They have forbidden organizers of a permitted rally in Queen's Park to use tables for literature, or chairs, or portable toilets.
My question therefore to the Deputy Prime Minister is this. Will he ask the Prime Minister to use his good offices with the Metro Toronto police so that, according to custom, the Metro police will enable the protesters to carry on a normal, peaceful protest on the streets of Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Janies Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can advise the Hon. Member that I have kept in touch with security matters for this conference. I receive daily briefings on it. Indeed, I am attending in Toronto tomorrow for a further review. I will certainly be prepared to bring the matter up, and ask them to review the matter for me. But I am certainly not prepared to make any commitments. However, we will look at it.


Oral Questions CITIZEN'S RIGHTS

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the Solicitor General. Will he on behalf of the Prime Minister declare publicly that the people of Toronto are free to exercise their normal right of free and peaceful public protest on the streets of Toronto outside the summit security area?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can advise the Hon. Member that the precautions we are taking for this economic summit are commensurate with the risks as perceived by our intelligence. While we have no specific threats at this time in any respect, I said before and I will say again that there is a high level of risk. We must be very careful and make sure that nothing untoward happens which would damage the reputation of Canada, not to say the lives of the people involved.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF BRITISH PENSIONERS LIVING IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Over 50,000 British pensioners live in Canada, and some 6,000 Canadian pensioners are currently residing in Britain. The lack of a social security agreement between our two countries, however, means that their pensions remain frozen at the amount set when persons moved out of their own country. No adjustment is allowed for cost of living increases.
Can the Minister tell the House what, if any, progress has been made to secure a social security agreement between our two countries so that the pensions of these important citizens will begin to reflect the yearly cost of living increases?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF BRITISH PENSIONERS LIVING IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very much interested in getting an agreement with the Government of the United Kingdom. There are approximately 76,000 people who would be eligible for it.
I should mention that when the Government came into office we had six such agreements. We now have approximately 18.
I can tell the House that, as early as October 9, 1984, we made contact with the United Kingdom in order that an agreement could be reached. I cannot go through all the details other than to say that in 1986 Canada and Australia joined in an effort to convey to the U.K. Government that an agreement was absolutely necessary, keeping in mind that there is an agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States.
As recently as January of this year when I met with the Right Hon. John Moore I made this case again, and we will do so further.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE SYSTEM
REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before time runs out, I would like to put a question to the Solicitor General. It concerns the announcements he made yesterday regarding parole.
The Solicitor General is trying to hoodwink Canadians into believing that something is being done to address the very serious problems in our criminal justice system. Rather than introducing legislation to deal in a comprehensive fashion with parole and sentencing in Canada, the Solicitor General is announcing proposals that will not affect the over 12,000 inmates who are presently in federal penitentiaries, and will not take effect for four or five years.
If the Solicitor General is truly concerned about the criminal justice system, and if the Conservative Government truly wants to take action, why are we not dealing with legislation rather than mere proposals?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the previous Government, this Government believes in consultation with the provinces, our provincial colleagues, with the member groups out there who are interested in this, and consultation with the standing committee.
We intend to proceed with that. It is my expectation and hope that following that consultation I will be able to introduce some legislation this summer.
I do not consider that that is an unreasonable period of time.

Mr. Speaker, that is absolute nonsense and the Solicitor General knows it. This Government has been in office for four years and we have not had any meaningful reform to the criminal justice system.
When is the Solicitor General going to address some of the immediate problems in federal penitentiaries? For example, last year in Ontario alone 280 federal inmates were referred for psychiatric assessment. The system was only able to accommodate 118.
If the Solicitor General is truly concerned about public safety, will he today commit the necessary resources in order to ensure that all federal inmates who require psychiatric assessment and treatment will receive that treatment before


they are released into society in order to ensure that society is duly protected?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can advise the Hon. Member again, as I did yesterday before the standing committee, that I asked the new Commissioner of Correctional Services of Canada to look into this on an urgent basis.
I wish to reassure the Hon. Member that indeed I am concerned about the safety of Canadians, because presently 60 per cent of the people incarcerated in our system are there for crimes against persons. That is why we are concerned about the safety of Canadians. We are acting to do something about it, which is something the former Government never addressed its mind to.

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, we have been working diligently at every level to get an agreement. An agreement with the U.K. Government is absolutely essential, and it should be done. That is why we joined with Australia, for example.
We will again examine what the Hon. Member has stated, and see what other methods we could use, even with direct intervention, if that is possible, in order to see if we can get an agreement.
The Hon. Member is absolutely correct in showing the concern that she has. I just wish the Liberals sometimes would too.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege today in relation to the contents of Hansard on June 14, 1988. I draw the attention of
Privilege-Mr. Boudria
the House to pages 16427 and 16428 of Hansard in which you will recall, Sir, that my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) concerning the Department of Public Works.
As recorded in Hansard in reply to the question the Prime Minister stated: ".. . members of the Opposition in the Liberal Party have been doing is slander Mr. LaSalle and saying that he is guilty without... evidence... " Upon further questioning by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) who asked: "Who said that?", Hansard records the Prime Minister as replying: "Boudria", meaning myself.
In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Citation 320 states that the word "slander" and "slanderous" aimed at an Hon. Member is inappropriate and has been ruled unparliamentary by previous Speakers, namely, on August 8, 1960, as reported at page 7777 of Hansard.
On occasion I will ask questions in the House which are perhaps tough, and I will acknowledge that I do ask questions of the Government, as is, I believe, the role of every Member of the House to do. In asking those questions, I in no way slandered anyone, in my humble belief, and if it is the opinion of Members of the House that I have done so, even if it were true, which it is not, it could not be said in the House of Commons under the rules that this House has set for itself. If any Hon. Member, other than the Prime Minister were to make such a statement, he would be asked to withdraw, as is appropriate.
I would like to submit that no lesser behaviour should be acceptable from the Prime Minister. I now call upon the Speaker to request at the earliest opportunity that the Prime Minister withdraw these unfortunate remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to my hon. friend's point of privilege, the first comment I wish to make is that if, in fact, there had been slander, and I will address that in a minute, it is obviously no point of privilege. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) that it would be heard today. I requested him to put it over until today because I had other obligations later yesterday afternoon.
I apologize to the Minister of State because I did not bring that to his attention, and I should have.

Business of the House
know in order that this matter could have been dealt with by all concerned.

speechtext: There is no specific reference. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) named no specific person. He named the entire Liberal Party, which I think is appropriate. He did not name the Hon. Member.

speechtext: Even if he is the Prime Minister he is not allowed to use that kind of language here.

Get up and speak to it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to put in my grain of salt on this point of order which touches upon the privilege of one of my colleagues, specially since I was present when the events took place, and since I saw with my own eyes the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) make accusations, and given that along with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), as the record will show-the Leader of the Opposition and myself asked the Prime Minister on two occasions who he was referring to.
When the Prime Minister said, and that is also on the record in the official report:

What the Liberal Party has been doing is: "slander Mr. La Salle and saying that he is guilty without any evidence being brought forward". When we heard this, of course we were not happy because it is not true.
Second, we wanted to make sure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would say exactly what he meant, so our Leader is quoted as saying: "Who said that?" The Prime Minister further continued by saying:
This has been said by Liberals in the House of Commons, and that is a
disgraceful way to do it.
Then the Leader of the Opposition again asked, and I shouted too: "Who said that?" Then the Prime Minister is quoted in Hansard as saying: "Boudria". I know of only one Boudria in the House of Commons and he is sitting right here. He does not have the habit of slandering people.

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that on the very day of the incident I personally checked the videotaped recording of the debate in the House and it is clear, if Your Honour would care to look at the videotape, the electronic Hansard, that from his seat the Prime Minister accused the Hon. Member from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell by name, which by the way is unparliamentary: "Boudria" he said, calling him by his name!
So then, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that for the sake of maintaining order in this House and to ensure that proper respect is shown towards all Hon. Members, Your Honour has no other choice but to ask the Prime Minister to take the first opportunity to withdraw the disgraceful and unparliamentary words he used and to apologize to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will take the matter under advisement. Again, I apologize not only to the Minister of State but to other Members who may have been caught a little unawares by my bringing this matter. However, I want to make very clear that it was brought this morning rather than earlier, at my request and through the courtesy of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I will examine the matter and report back to the House.
I might add that the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) is unable to be here at the moment, but I hope that my remarks are extended to him and it may be that he wishes to address the Chair further.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it being Thursday, I would ask the Deputy Government House Leader if he would be kind enough to let us know what business the Government intends to bring before the House in the coming week.

speechtext:

the Parties that debate on all matters with respect to Bill C-55 will be completed tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Government House Leader has indicated the business for the next few days. There was some suggestion that we might, at an early date, get to the legislation amending the National Transportation Act concerning the disabled. There has been some discussion among the critics and the Parties. I thought this was coming quite soon. Could he give us an indication when the Government will move on that?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to indicate to the Member that we have been discussing various items of business with a hope that the House could proceed to do business. Unfortunately, my hon. friend has been introducing Bills and his Party has been calling for votes about whether or not he should be allowed to introduce the Bills. That blew all of yesterday.
If we can get through today and pass a motion to extend the sittings, I give my hon. friend the undertaking that that and other Bills are very high on our list of priorities. I would say to him, however, that in order to do business we have to get through Routine Proceedings. We have to get through those proceedings without dilatory motions and votes.
My hon. friend is the captain of that particular ship, under today's circumstances, the Routine Proceedings being constructed the way they are. If we get through Routine Proceedings today and get this motion passed, we will be on to Business of the House.
Yesterday my hon. friend's Party delayed him from introducing his own Bills. It was rather tragic, because one likes to think that the House Leader of a Party has his Party behind him and will stand with him when he wants to introduce one of his own Private Members' Bills. But that did not happen yesterday. That may very well be the case today.
When my hon. friend has his team with him and can get us through Routine Proceedings, we will proceed to Business of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I think there must be some mistake. First, I want to say that my caucus, by definition, is behind me on these matters. I want to make it perfectly clear that if the Deputy Government House Leader wishes to bring forward the Bill that would see amendments to the National Transportation Act to assist the disabled of Canada, we would pass that very quickly, perhaps within minutes. However, when Orders of the Day indicate there is no intention, at least today, of introducing that particular legislation or other good pieces of legislation, then one is less than interested in indicating some co-operation.
Business of the House
I want to indicate clearly that when that appears on the Order Paper he can count on at least one Party in the House moving expeditiously. That will be the New Democratic Party.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I and my Party do not want to play politics with amendments to the National Transportation Act for the disabled. If the motion to extend the sittings passes before six o'clock tonight, that item of business will be called immediately thereafter and we will need one short speech to introduce it and it will have second reading debate tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am glad to hear that both gentlemen would like to expedite things, but could you tell us why the clock shows the hour to be 6.15? Is someone trying to expedite matters in the House?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I probably should explain to Hon. Members that once again the clocks have been moving more rapidly than time itself. I wanted to comment earlier that after the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) rose on his question and received his answer, the clock registered that the entire exchange had taken an hour and a half.

Mr. Speaker, there is a Bill that we in the New Democratic Party are very interested in expediting. I did not hear the Deputy Government House Leader deal with it. It is Bill C-82 dealing with lobbying, which has been promised for three years now. It was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on an urgent basis. We have had first reading of the Bill. We are prepared to expedite that Bill because we believe, with the Prime Minister, that it is an urgent Bill and should be dealt with. I am waiting to find out when Bill C-82 will be brought for second reading.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend inadvertently referred to it as the Bill on lobbying. I believe Bill C-82 is the conflict of interest Bill.
Lobbyists.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: The Lobbyists Registration Act? That is at report stage. Yes, Bill C-82 is at report stage. It is on a list of Bills that we have agreed are priority Bills. Once we pass the motion to extend the hours and then move past the free trade legislation to the legislation we have agreed is priority legislation, legislation in which a great deal of time has been invested by Members of all Parties, we will debate it. It is on that priority list of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Deputy House Leader a further question on Business of the House. A few moments ago, when addressing the legislation that will be brought forward for tomorrow's agenda, the Minister mentioned Bill C-55, and I believe he intimated that there was unanimous agreement to the passage of Bill C-55 through all stages. If that is the case, I would ask the Deputy House Leader to clarify the situation, because I know that on our side, there was no consent to do that. It was


Privilege-Mr. Orlikow
our understanding that Bill C-55 was being brought forward tomorrow and that Members of Parliament would address it and participate in the debate, but there was no agreement given by the Liberal caucus to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Friesen) that we would agree to passage through all stages tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I happen to have my notes still, and the wording I used was, "I believe that there is an understanding among the Parties that the debate will be completed Friday". If that is not the case, then I think I am still covered by my words. If I had had a firm understanding, I would have said that there is a firm understanding, but those are the words I used.
This Bill has been before the Elouse for some time. There was considerable debate on it at second reading stage and considerable time was spent on it in committee. The Senate delayed it for a long, long time. I would hope that my hon. friend would see his way clear to help the Government complete its consideration of the Senate amendments so that this very important legislation could be passed.

In response to my hon. friend's comments, there is no agenda on this side of the House to prolong the debate any longer than is necessary. One of the problems with the way this Bill has been brought forward has been the mad rush in the last number of days to bring upon the House an inordinate number of Bills.
Bill C-55 has had a roller-coaster ride. It has been introduced one day, yanked off the list for the next three or four days, and then put back on the list. I would suggest that a number of Members from all sides would like to address themselves to the Senate amendments to Bill C-55. It is not simply a question of prolonging debate. The fact is that the debate on the Senate amendments to Bill C-55 has not taken a long time.
Tomorrow, if Members of Parliament wish to address themselves to Bill C-55, we would like to give them the opportunity to do so, as opposed simply to saying that there is an understanding that the debate will end tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of proceedings in and decisions made by the legislative committee dealing with Bill C-129 this morning. The committee began its consideration of the Bill on Tuesday. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) appeared before the committee and made a presentation. We had an opportunity to question him.
On Tuesday, the Chairman of the committee asked Hon. Members who wished to submit a list of names of possible witnesses who would be invited to appear before the committee to bring that list this morning. I came to the meeting this morning with a relatively short list of witnesses including people representing the unions, the workers of Air Canada, several academics who are expert in the field of transportation and some people from-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know that the Hon. Member is a very experienced Member in this place and is expressing a complaint. I do not think the Chair needs to have a long list of all the witnesses he or anyone else would propose, but I would like to know what exactly it is that happened which goes to the question of privilege, which of course is something happening which makes it impossible for the Hon. Member to carry on his duties as a Member of Parliament, keeping in mind that we have a long-standing rule and many judgments indicating that unless it is something extraordinary indeed, the committee is master of its own destiny. Keeping that in mind, I would ask the Hon. Member to focus very carefully on his exact point.

Mr. Speaker, the Chairman ruled, and the committee accepted his decision, that all the witnesses, some suggested by me and some suggested by the Liberal member from Cape Breton, be heard in one day. I suggest that that ruling breaches my privileges, and I have several citations from Beauchesne's which I think confirm my view.
Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Fifth Edition, says in Citation 77 on page 24 the following:
Witnesses before committees share the same privilege of freedom of speech as Members.
I would ask you to consider whether the restricting of evidence of those to be called before the committee to one day is not an abridgement of their freedom of speech. They will certainly not get the same consideration nor time that would occur if normal scheduling were allowed.
I would also ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider that the constriction on our ability to question these witnesses also constitutes an abridgement of our freedom of speech. Citation 55 on page 20 of Beauchesne's reads:
-"that the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place outside of Parliament".
This suggests that the members of the majority should not suppress the free speech of the members of the minority. I suggest that to insist that all witnesses be heard on one day and that the clause-by-clause discussion be completed in one day breaches my privileges and those of other Members of Parliament.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I attended the meeting of the legislative committee on Bill C-129 concerning the privatization of Air


Canada. Representations were made by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), by the Member representing the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-North (Mr. Orlikow) and also by the government. And in all three cases, the list of witnesses presented was not retained in its entirety. The Parties present gave their consent and the assistant to the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys was there. I cannot see how the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-North can have been denied his rights. The committee felt that a certain number of witnesses should be heard and therefore decided to have four sessions to hear witnesses during the same day, which is the same, Mr. Speaker, as having one committee sit during four days.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). What he said has a great deal of validity, and it is a cause for concern to me.
Your Honour will recall that we had a debate recently about what was considered notice on second reading of Bill C-129. Since completion of second reading, it has gone to committee. A meeting was called for Monday to set up the committee. I was unable to be at the meeting, but my assistant was there and was told that the Minister was going to appear before the committee the next day. The committee had not even been formed but evidently the Government had made its opinion known to the chairman and set it up so that the Minister was going to be there the following day. It is a pleasure to have the Minister there at any time, but I think the Government should be a little more careful and not schedule meetings until the committee is formed.
The meeting to which the Hon. Member refers was at eight o'clock this morning. I was coming back from my constituency and unable to be there for the meeting, but as it turns out, all the witnesses are now scheduled for next Tuesday. One of the witnesses to whom I was speaking is very upset. He feels his rights are being violated because he cannot be there on a certain day and he cannot be a witness on Bill C-129.
There has to be a fair way of dealing with this without infringing on the democratic process.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have to say to Hon. Members that I am having a great deal of difficulty accepting this as a question of privilege. However, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who has been here for many years and contributed much to this place, in putting his procedural argument, brought up one quote from Beauchesne's which I want to look at very carefully. If I feel it is necessary I will return to the Chamber, but I want to emphasize again that there is a very fundamental rule in this place that unless it is something extraordinary indeed, it is not for the Chair to interfere with the majority decision of a committee.
We will now move on to other matters.
